newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - East Europe uranium mines a costly peril.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - East Europe uranium mines a costly peril.

text.p: Robert Egri, 54, looks every inch the absent-minded professor in his white coat, peering into steaming vats of liquefied uranium ore.
Egri's job is to help keep the crumbling Hungarian mill stable until the time comes to close it and level the plant.
Officials say the Cold War relic could threaten drinking water of the nearby city of Pecs.
It must be shut down -- at enormous cost.
"I took part in the buildup and my profession is that of radiochemist," Egri said, standing on a catwalk.
"Many years ago these buildings were very nice but now we spend almost nothing on them," he said.
"The money is just enough for production -- to keep it stable just to the end," Egri said, noting that many of the 132 buildings were slightly contaminated and would have to be destroyed.
The Mecsek Ore Mining Company was once a vital source of uranium "yellow cake" for Soviet nuclear weapons. It is expected to ship out its last uranium consignment next year.
Mecsek, in southwest Hungary, is like many former Soviet uranium mines and mills dotted throughout eastern Europe -- uneconomical, outmoded and environmentally hazardous.

"I'm not telling you anything if I tell you the Soviets did not care much about the environment," said Bernard Griepink, director of environmental projects for PHARE, an EU-sponsored assistance programme for former East-bloc countries.
Mines like Mecsek were built in great secrecy and often with forced labour, wherever the Soviets found uranium deposits.
Its purpose originally was disguised by calling it a bauxite mine and workers say it was overseen by the Soviet KGB.

Mecsek has become Hungary's problem by default since the collapse of the Soviet Union. But officials in Western Europe have realised that shutting the former East bloc's uranium operations is too costly and too important to be left to the cash-strapped countries themselves.
"There has been a lot of mining in eight or nine countries in eastern Europe and some are continuing," said Jan Vrijen, coordinator of PHARE's uranium mining remediation project.
"The biggest problem is in those countries where activities have been closed down. Suddenly some four or five years ago after they opened the borders they saw the real market prices."
Mecsek produces refined uranium at $60 per kilo (2.2 pounds) while the world price is about $30 a kilo, officials said.
"It's because of the geological problems, the depth of the mines and the relatively low uranium content," said Istvan Benkovics, Mecsek's general director.
"We never produced at world market prices. Because of the strict Russian influence, there was a price in the West and a price in the East. It was two separate markets."

Bulgaria, supplier of uranium for the first Soviet atomic bomb, started to wind down production in 1991 and has 55 sites to contend with. The Balkan state, whose economy is in a state of collapse, needs two billion levs ($8.02 million) in 1997 alone for rehabilitation.
Officials doubt the government has the money.

Officials from the Czech Republic, once a cornerstone of Soviet uranium production, say the country has 500 "uranium liabilities" -- running the gamut from mines to tailing ponds to mills. The country needs $25 million a year for many years to come to decommission them, Czech officials said.

Romania has mines and mills while Estonia has no mines but had one of the Soviet bloc's biggest mills. Poland had uranium mining for only a few years, but it stopped and the records were scattered to the winds, complicating cleanup.

Hungary, by comparison, is lucky. It has only the Mecsek mine and mill, but closing the operation is expected to cost 12 billion forints ($75.5 million) to 14 billion forints ($88 million), and some 1,000 miners will lose their jobs, mine officials said.
Mecsek is still producing, using sulphuric acid to leach uranium from the crushed ore, pumping the acid, mixed with heavy salts and some uranium and radon, into two tailing ponds.

There is no immediate threat to Pecs's drinking water, but a company environmental report says dissolved salts pumped into the ponds have infiltrated the ground water, "causing potential danger for the nearby drinking water reserves".
Ducks occasionally land on the ponds, lured by the warmth, but they don't stay long because nothing lives there -- the salts kill everything but the plants.
Officials say the potential threat to drinking water is the greatest hazard posed by most eastern uranium mines and mills.
"The major concern is the groundwater," Vrijen said.

"We need a good knowledge of where the wastes are, whether they have potential for harm and, secondly, to find out what can they do to the groundwater and where does the groundwater connect to the drinking water."
Mecsek's Benkovics says potential contamination of drinking water is a major concern, but the problem can be alleviated by water treatment and other means, if enough money is available.
PHARE can help, with expertise and consultants, but the bulk of costs must be borne by the countries themselves, PHARE officials said.
"PHARE is some help, but it is not significant compared to the real budget," Benkovics said.
